Robert Glasper

Pianist and composer Robert Glasper has demonstrated one path that the 21st century jazz artist can follow. His melding of R&B, hip hop and jazz has proved highly successful, both critically and in the marketplace. Robert has collaborated with a diverse list of artists including Terence Blanchard, Christian McBride, Kanye West and MeShell Ndegeocello and he currently leads his own piano trio.
Robert was interviewed in Clinton, NY on February 20, 2016 by Greg Thomas, Hamilton class of ‘85.

MR: Thanks for coming early for this, I’m sure it’s going to be a great concert. This is Greg Thomas, class of ’85 and he was in the jazz program, he was in the jazz band and he’s been here for a few days. He had a great lecture the other day. And Robert Glasper, who you all know. He’s got his trio. And I’m going to turn things over to Greg and they’re going to just chat for a while and see what they come up with.
Thank you, Monk. And welcome everyone. Thank you for coming to hear this pre- concert chat. How you doing, man?
Good. I had about a five, six hour drive up here.
Oh. From the City?
Yeah, from New York, yeah, from Brooklyn.

Okay. Gotcha. All right. So as you were mentioning off camera, about I guess five months ago there was an event at which I interviewed Mr. Glasper, it was an event sponsored by the National Jazz Museum in Harlem, it was a jazz and R&B discussion. So that was quite cool, and that was in front of an audience of music students at your alma mater, the New School.
Right. Uh huh.

So we went into some kind of musical depth into your history. Here I’d like to direct it for the students here and the students looking. Some of the questions that I ask will be kind of directed towards them and where they’re at. All right. So the first question I have for you has to do with the fact that you have a very identifiable voice and style as a band leader, as a performer, as a musician, even as a composer. And I’d like you to talk about the importance of an individual voice. Because you know in the music’s history, that was like the thing. That used to be the thing. It’s like you’ve got to have it, your voice.
Totally.

But in music schools when you have, instead of it being on the bandstand and through traveling on the road with big bands and that type of thing where it was an apprenticeship process, now that you have a lot of music schools it seems to be more of a — not a © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-

cookie cutter, but less — maybe cookie cutter. Maybe less of the individuality. So could you talk about that? Because I think the young people here, they — I think they need to hear about the importance of that.

Yeah, totally. It’s — the music in schools is good and bad, you know what I mean? For the most part it’s good because if there wasn’t music in schools I wouldn’t be sitting here, you know, I’d be somewhere in Houston at somebody’s church, playing in church, being that cat that’s really good in Houston, you know? But I was able to get a full scholarship to go to college, to go up to New York, you know. So that’s why, I made it there. I mean Miles Davis went to music school. I mean that’s the good thing about school. It gets you where you need to be. You know like some people don’t get ahead in life simply because of where they are.
Geographically.

Because of the geographical thing, not because of a talent thing or anything like that. They’re just not — you’ve got to move where the food is or else you’re going to be hungry. It’s simple. You know so many people have said that, like, “I’m hungry.” And I’m like, “you need to go where the food is.” You know? And then they don’t want to take the sacrifice to do it and it can be hard. But luckily if there’s school it takes some of that padding out, it makes it less hard, because of school. And then when you’re grown it’s like move to New York and you have nothing. Then it’s like a little bit harder because now where are you going to live, there’s no dormitory and nothing like that. You’re grown now so it’s a little harder. But for me school was the thing. And, you know, a lot of times with schools, you know you have teachers in the schools, most of the time, that, a lot of them are sometimes failed musicians and you know what I mean? They can teach but they can’t teach you how to be yourself. You know what I mean? Some schools have great teachers like that. New School had great teachers like that. They actually have teachers that were on amazing records. Like one of my teachers was Reggie Workman. You know? What else do you need?
John Coltrane.

Right. Charlie Persip, you know? I had cats teaching me that played with Bird. You know what I mean? So that’s a different thing. Because they were around all those individual cats and they understand the thing. They’re not failed musicians or anything, they’re in schools because they want to teach us, give us what they know. Not because that’s all they got. And so before music became a music business per se, it was really cool to be yourself and have your own voice. And that’s what it was about. Who’s different? That’s why so many different groups and even individual artists, you’re looking in the 60s or 70s and the 80s, there were so many different kinds of artists looking different, sounding different, the music was different, blah-blah-blah, and everybody can make it. Nowadays © Fillius Jazz Archive -3-

it’s literally like three artists you’ve got to fit in that mold. If you’re a black singer and you are a male you’ve got to fit somewhere in the Chris Brown mold. You know? If you’re female you’ve got to fit in the Beyoncé mold. You know I went to high school with Beyoncé. So that’s another individual that I know — I knew her for a long time. You know. But those are certain molds that people say okay, now we need you to be like that because that makes money, versus people taking the time. You know they used to even have a thing called Artist Development in record labels. They would sign somebody and put you through the wringer to help you figure out how to do shows and be on stage, talk to the press, all these things. Now they just sign you and throw you out there. Because they just want to make the quick dollar. Especially now, because record labels are folding and all that. So that don’t have no time for no artist development, they don’t care. You know? But you know the artists that have the individual voice are the artists that last. And those are the artists that people remember. You know, that’s just a real thing.
I think relative to the students, it’s really important for them to think about the same things for themselves.

Totally. Yeah. And it’s hard to be like, “have your individual voice. Go!” You know. It’s like I didn’t know I had a voice until people started telling me, “yo man, I was at a rehearsal and the cat was like, ‘yo man, gimme that like a Glasper kind of sound.’” You know. I remember when I first heard that. I was in college.
Oh wow. That’s cool.

I was actually — was I still in college? I was still in college but I was like a senior in college and there was like some of the cats at the school were having rehearsal for something and somebody told me like, “hey using that Glasper sound.” I was like, “wow, really?” That sound? Cool. You know what I mean?
And sometimes somebody else has to actually tell you.

They have to tell you you have a sound because you don’t really realize you have a sound until somebody tells you. Then you go, “oh snap. Maybe I do have a sound.” You know. But other than that it’s like, “oh, I do.” You know, and then you start realizing, like I started realizing through the years people were saying, “your compositions are different. They’re kind of not like” blah-blah-blah-blah, “they kind of have this feel to it.” And I realized what I did is, you know I grew up in church and I never ignored my influences. You know what I mean? So, especially when I’m writing music. When I’m making a composition of my own I never ignore my church influence or my R&B. You know my mom was a singer. I grew up in clubs. You know she didn’t let babysitters watch me. She would take me to — I was three years old at the club you know, in the room in the back. You know, so she could check on me between songs you know. “You all right? All © Fillius Jazz Archive -4-

right.” [sings] “I’m every woman.” You know. So I grew up with all these sounds, and going to rehearsals and everything, and so when I got into jazz and I pretty much got in and really starting like delving into jazz when I was in ninth grade or maybe eighth grade. And when I got into that, you know, what I did was I learned how to play it authentically, because I wanted to sound like Oscar Peterson. I loved Oscar Peterson. My mom used to play him in the house all the time. So I used to try my best to sound like Oscar. I transcribed solos and all these things. So I learned how to play the music authentically. But when it came to writing my own music, I always let my influences influence me. I would give this out. Like this is what I heard you know, and it wouldn’t have the normal chord progressions that the average jazz, the normal jazz 2-5-1s they call it, and all that stuff, well it wouldn’t be there. It would be something else.
Or A-A-B-A.

A-A-B-A, all that stuff. I wrote from my hip-hop sensibility a lot of the times. You know. I would have a bridge, you know, and it wouldn’t be like A-A-B-A, it would be like A-B- C, then a D, then I’d go back to an A. I said, “wait, that’s not 32 bars.” That’s not the normal thing. And so for me I kept that. Because that was who I was. You know what I mean? And when I say that, I don’t want people to get it twisted, because sometimes when I say, “let your influences influence you,” that doesn’t mean everything you play sounds like you’re from church. You know what I mean? Because that happens.
That can happen?
Most of the time that happens.
Because that influence is so strong.

It’s so strong to where they don’t learn to separate it when they’re playing a jazz tune you don’t have to sound like you’re from church. Like church progressions. There are certain things whereas like okay, this is a church cat. Because everything is a church progression, everything is this, everything sounds like you’re in praise or worship. And that’s not supposed to happen all the time.
Right.

When you’re writing your own music, fine. If that’s what you’re hearing. But when you’re in a specific context playing, you know, in a jazz context you have to know when to turn that off and when to turn it on.
That’s very interesting. You saying this. Because to me it brings up the issue of genres.
Yup.
So for you, you grew up hearing all of this.
Um hum.

You were exposed to it, you were around it, you ended up playing it. So as I said to you back in September, when I listen to your music and I hear you and I see you going in © Fillius Jazz Archive -5-

these different areas, even when I frankly didn’t even know the extent of your musical associations with Bilal and this one and Mos Def. I didn’t really know that. But I was like this is organic. It wasn’t a trick. It wasn’t a marketing ploy.
Right.
Sometimes you can hear somebody and it doesn’t sound like it really came from their heart.
Right.
You know what I mean?
Yeah, totally.
But with you it was like, I was like, well yeah, I can hear that. The cat can play but he’s doing that, he’s doing this.
And with all my influences I actually live in those worlds musically.
Simultaneously.

Simultaneously. That’s why I can, that’s why I feel like I play them well, because I literally was on the road with the masters of their craft. You know what I mean? So like I say I played damn near my whole life in church, so that’s one part. But then when I got to New York pretty much as soon as I got to New York, you know, I was in the company of Common and Q-Tip and Mos Def and all those guys, and I started in the Roots. And Questlove used to call me to play with the Roots when I was in college a lot. Then after college I played with them a lot. So now I’m in the hip-hop world and I’m playing that. I’m watching James Poyser and I’m playing all these hip-hop tracks now and learning how to play that vibe. You know, that’s the vibe. I get it. Boom-boom-boom.
But each genre has a particular vibe.

Each genre has a particular vibe and it’s very egotistical — a lot of jazz musicians think because they have a lot of chops that every other music is easy to play and you can just do it. But that’s not the case.

Well T.S. Monk, Thelonious Monk’s son, who for years played in R&B, he made it very clear, he’s like, you know, you’re playing that? Can you keep that time right there? Can you keep it there? Can you keep it there like that?
Right. Bum-bum-be. Yeah. That’s T.S. That’s my cousin-in-law.
Oh yeah?
Yeah.
Oh okay. Small world.
Small world. So yeah, so basically I went through the training camp of each of those genres of music you know what I mean, basically. In a way.
So then that’s how in a way, you’re a producer.
Right. © Fillius Jazz Archive -6-
Which means that you have the ability to be able to — well let me let you explain. Now you mentioned yourself as a composer, as a player. As a producer, explain how you see your role as a producer.
I mean as a producer, as far as my own stuff or producing other people?
Other people.
Well as a producer the thing a great producer is supposed to do is bring the best out of that person, what they are.
Like great teachers do.
Yeah, exactly. Bring, you know, some producers, when they produce something you hear it and you’re like okay so-and-so produced that. I hear it.
Mmm. You could hear the stamp of the producer.

Hear the stamp of the producer. Which is not always bad. You know you hear something Babyface did, you’re like, “that’s Babyface.” You know? Duh. That’s Face. You know. You get it. That’s R. Kelly. You know? Certain producers have a thing, and some people want that thing. Because that thing sells and that’s what — you kind of want people to know that’s you, and that’s a different kind of producing. But from what I’m doing, I like to bring the best out of that particular artist, so I try to dwell in what they — where they live and figure that out and then go from there.
Quincy does that, right?

Yeah, Quincy does that. Exactly. Exactly. They didn’t want Quincy producing Michael [Jackson] because he was a jazz guy. They didn’t want him doing “Off the Wall.” Michael had to fight for Quincy to do “Off the Wall,” because he was the jazz guy. He never really did R&B like that you know. And boom.
History was made.
History was made.
Now tell us about your collaboration with Kendrick Lamar on “To Pimp a Butterfly.”

Yeah, Kendrick, first of all a lot of my friends are on that, are producers on that, on all the Kendrick stuff from “Section.80” and “good kid, m.A.A.d. city” and all his records. One in particular, Terrace Martin, a producer, I went to jazz camp with Terrace in high school, when I was 15 years old, and we met each other then. He’s in L.A. He’s from L.A. and we all met at Loyola in New Orleans, they had like a national high school jazz band thing. We were both in there. So we kept in touch all through the years. And he used to call me up to do Snoop Dogg tours and stuff, because he was Snoop Dog’s music director too. I was never around to do them. As soon as I got in college I pretty much went on the road with Christian McBride and Russell Malone and Terence and a few other people.
Terence Blanchard. © Fillius Jazz Archive -7-
Terence Blanchard. So I was never really at school very much. Especially my sophomore year on I was gone a lot.
Okay. And it’s good to go to a school that —
That allows you to do that. Yeah. I still had to fight. Some of them teachers was wishing they was on the gig.
No, you be in class.

Right. But I’m playing at the Vanguard for a week. But most of the teachers were super cool about that, and the New School was really cool about that. That’s the thing. That’s what you’re there for. You know. So anyway fast forward, I heard “good kid, m.A.A.d city” and it blew me away. And I called Terrace and I was like, “yup, I have to be on the next CD somehow,” to be on Kendrick’s next album. He’s like, “gotcha. We gonna make it happen.” I was like, “aye, bet.” And so fast forward I’m doing my trio album, “Covered” — I put out last year.
This was your last recording.

My last recording. And I’m in L.A. And that’s the thing about going where the food is, because L.A. is one of those places where there’s a lot of food. So I did two recording nights there. The first night I go, I’m recording at Studio A. I recorded it live in the studio at Capitol Records. In Studio B was John Mayer recording his record. He walks over, he’s like, “hey, Robert.” We’d never met in person. He’s like, “Robert, what’s up?” I go, “hey man, I’ve never met you” blah-blah-blah. He was like, “after you finish your recording, you want to come over to my studio and jam?” I’m like, “aright.” So I finished my recording and I went next door and jammed with John Mayer for two hours. Duo. Just me and him. You know? At the studio on tape.
On tape?
On tape, yeah.
All right.
So I don’t know if anybody will come up with anything, but, that happened. It was like that was pretty awesome.
Cool.

The second night, before I walked on to play, Terrace called me, he was like, “yo, I’m at the studio, at Dr. Dre’s studio. Can you come here right after you finish your session?” I was like, “aright.” So this is the funny part about this whole thing. I go in, I finish my recording session, mind you “Covered” is a trio album but it’s not straight ahead jazz. You know we’re pretty much doing cover songs and it’s not [scats] you know. As soon as I go to the Dr. Dre studio, I walk in, Kendrick’s there, I didn’t even know what I was going for. Terrace is like, “Kendrick this is Rob” boom-boom-boom-boom. He was like, © Fillius Jazz Archive -8-
“I want you to play on some joints.” I was like, “cool.” The first song was [scats a swing groove].
Love it. Love it. The irony of that.
The irony of that. I go from a jazz session playing hip-hop to a hip-hop session playing jazz.
Love it. Love it.

And so the first thing, Terrace is like, this first tune I want you to sound like McCoy Tyner. You know? It was a song called “For Free.” And Kendrick’s like doing a poem over it and we’re swinging and like going in. You know what I mean?
Right. Oh yeah.

So I was like this is so random. So then after I did that song Kendrick pulled up a bunch of other songs that they already recorded. And he was like, “hey could you hear anything over this?” He’d be playing and I’d be like, figure it out, record. He’s like, “play anything you hear.” And I’d just play. He was like, “killing.” No pull up so-and-so, pull up so-and- so. I sat there and I recorded eight songs in one sitting, right there, just that night.
Didn’t send him the charts.

No charts. No I just played it and I listened to it. Thundercat was there too so some of the songs he wrote he came in and showed me the joint, I learned it and then he would record and I would just like play what I heard, you know? And so there was nine songs on the album. So I came back Grammy week, because we were nominated for Black Radio 2 at that time. And so I came back Grammy week and that’s when we did the “Mortal Man” the very last song with the Tupac interview on it. That’s when I recorded that. But yeah, I’m on nine joints. It’s only credited five songs. Because after I did what I did, you know, months after that they forgot what I played on, you know, hip-hop. That’s one of the things with hip-hop you don’t get your business right.
Right.
But I’m on there. But anyway it was just an amazing opportunity and it was the irony of, like you say, going from the jazz session playing hip-hop, to the hip-hop session playing jazz.
I love it. Love it.
And it’s just full. You know what I mean?

So describe your process. Let’s go to your trio, of arranging. I listened to — I purposely did this, I listened to “Covered” and then I went back to your first two joints with the trio so I could hear — and it’s identifiable. But with “Covered” that seems like some intricate arrangements and textures. You know, you always set up a groove but then there are surprises in there all over the place. So describe your process of arranging when you’re © Fillius Jazz Archive -9-
with your cats. And I also want you to tell us the two cats that you’ll be playing with today, how far you all go back.

Oh Damion Reid and Vicente Archer. The trio. I go back with them since 2000. Yeah 2000. Not two thousand and, two thousand. I met Damion in college, the drummer, in college. But the process with them is pretty much — on those other albums, those earlier albums were just original, mostly original songs. And I like to write for those particular musicians in that seat.
That Duke Ellington vibe.

Yeah, exactly. That’s why Duke’s band is different from any other band. Because he wrote for the cats that were there. You know, he had these people in mind so the whole thing has a sound and a characteristic versus writing just the drum chair, the piano chair, this chair, that chair. You write for a specific person. And you don’t write a lot. Because I don’t like to write a lot of stuff. I like to let that particular musician give me him. You know what I mean? Like when I write for Vicente or when I write for Derrick Hodge in my experiment band, when I’m writing something or when I hear Derrick doing him I’m like oh my God, he’s going to kill this. So I don’t want to write, “play specifically this.” Sometimes writers can do that and, for me, when I do that with my bands it kind of puts it in a box and it can be bigger than what I’m thinking almost. Because whey they’re going to do is going to be better than what I’m going to tell them to do.
So what do you actually write?
It’s trust I use. What I write —
I mean for them.

For them, I mean for the most part I’ll tell them a skeleton, like, depending on the song, obviously there are some songs I have that in the trio days that specific bass line I would write. But then I would be like get away from it and do you, and let the drummer kind of feel. Like it’s in seven, this is kind of the vibe, go for what you hear. You know what I mean? So it’s a mixture of that. Some things I’m specific on because I have to be specific because I have a certain thing I’m going for, but even in that I give them room to interpret it a little bit. I don’t do specifically every little thing. You know what I mean? And to me that’s how you have the best groups, that’s when it’s a group. Because you’re letting each person bring their personality into the music and no other band’s going to sound like these exact three people. You know what I mean? Versus you writing something for this or another person. I could go to another band and do the same thing and then it sounds the same because you’re doing exactly — you’re reading the music and you’re doing exactly what I need you to do, but I like to — you give me your feel, you give me your feel [claps] and then it’s going to sound like something like no other cats sound like. You know? That’s what Miles did. Miles was the best at that. Miles — © Fillius Jazz Archive -10-

that’s one thing he was a master at. Miles was the master at finding the right guys. He didn’t change. You know? Miles never really changed as far as his playing. He just got the right cats under him because he knew what sound he was going for and he was like, okay, these young guys know the vibe boom-boom-boom-boom we’ll try the young vibe and then put my thing on top of it. And that was something.
Did you hear the story about when Miles first got Herbie, Tony, Ron and Wayne together?
Which one?

Yeah right. I think this is the one where they first went to his house. And he was in another room. And they didn’t know that he was listening to them from the other room. But he was just checking them out.
Right. Right. Right. Right. Right. That makes sense. Yeah. That totally makes sense.
Yeah. Like a master of masters, teacher of teachers. I mean so many leaders came from Miles.
Um hum. Exactly.

Now I’m going to ask one more question then you all get ready because I’m going to let you all get in here. I want to talk about tradition and continuity of tradition. I did a presentation here on the great writer about blues and jazz, Albert Murray. And one of the things he says in his book The Hero and the Blues is that of course tradition is that which continues. That’s obvious. But he says if the tradition is not — this is my paraphrase — renewed then the tradition can atrophy. So you actually need change for the tradition to remain alive.

A tradition is change also. You know what I mean? What is a tradition? When you think of a tradition as — that’s why people talk to me about that stuff, about you don’t even know what you’re talking about from the beginning, your question don’t even make sense. Why don’t you keep more of the tradition? Which tradition? Which era? Which one? The thirties? Because when the forties hit, that was something different. When the fifties hit, that was something different. When the sixties hit, each era looked back on the other era, or looked ahead at the other era like, “what are you doing? That’s not the tradition.” You know? They all did that. The thirties looked at the forties like what are you doing? The forties looked at the fifties, what are you doing? And like the sixties, what are you doing? That’s the tradition. If you’re not making the other era mad you’re not following the tradition. Your tradition is to piss you off.
Or in the academy they call it paradigm shifts.

Yeah, yeah, yeah, exactly. But that is the tradition. The tradition is to honor the history but not be held back by the history. And you keep it moving. You keep it moving. But you honor it and you know it’s there, you pay homage to it but you keep it moving. © Fillius Jazz Archive -11-
Because that’s the only way to keep it alive. Miles said it. If it ain’t moving it’s dead. Period.

All right. I see a lot of heads shaking out there. So why don’t you all get up in this, all right? So if you’ve got a question or a comment raise your hand and partake. All right. This is Professor Michael “Doc” Woods, Professor of Music here for many years.
Hello, sir. Nice to meet you.
Great composer, bassist.

I’ll bet you’re a musician. MW: Your church background I think is just fabulous. Do you see any way in the immediate future on your event horizon where you can kind of revolutionize, particularly in black churches, what the black pastors will let the young musicians do?

I think that’s already changing. Granted, they kicked me out of church in ’99. Footnote, I got kicked out. But thank God, when I was playing in church in Houston when I got a scholarship to come to New York, my pastor in Houston led this church called Brentwood Baptist Church, and my pastor said, “I’m going to call my boy up in Harlem and you’re going to play at his church when you get there.” So I had a good job the first week I got to New York. I got to New York, they put me over to the male chorus first of all, I’m 17 or 18 years old over the male chorus, I’m like, “no!” They were horrible, it was really bad. And then a few months after that they put me on the teen choir so it was like yes. So the teen choir was cool. At that point I started getting calls from, like I said, Christian McBride and I started going out of town. And at that point it wasn’t cool to go out of town. I mean you’ve got to be at church. So after a while it was like I had to make a decision, to be here or not. So I said I had to leave. It’s now become cool for your music director to be gone, because the pastor can say, “our music director is out with Mary J. Blige this Sunday.” You know. And when you get back from tour, all my friends that still play in church tell me that, I’ve got a bunch of cats that play with everybody and the pastor comes back and, “so our bassist just got back from the road from the Beyoncé tour.” So it makes it hard — it gives the church a little popping thing. Who did your piano player play for? You know. So I think now it’s become a lot more acceptable. You know what I mean? And you know I think that’s just the culture now. You know? You do other stuff and I play at this church. It’s almost like giving the church publicity when you’re on the road a lot of times. Because the people want to kind of — the people want to go to the church that has the really good music as well. The younger people tend to want to go to the church with good music. Older people want to go to church for the good preacher. So if you have both it’s great. The best choir, the best musicians get a lot of the younger people. You know what I mean? So if the word on the street is, you know, “Maxwell’s band plays over here.” Then all right. You know. Then that works. I mean © Fillius Jazz Archive -12-

I’ve played with Maxwell for five years, and in 2009 when he came back with “Pretty Wings” and all that stuff, so I did that tour, from ’09 to 2013, and my boy Shedrick Mitchell was on organ on a church gig every Sunday. But he was telling me, that’s why I know a lot of these things because he was like he said, “yeah my pastor — I always sang that stuff — it fascinates people.” But I thought you were going to ask me if I was going to do a Gospel album. What’s the highlight of your career thus far? And is there another “Black Radio” coming or in the works?

The highlight of my career. I would probably say winning my first Grammy and it being an R&B Grammy. You know, for “Black Radio,” the original “Black Radio” album. I think that was the highlight pinnacle of my career because that’s like winning the NBA championship, you know, if you are a basketball player and you win the championship that’s the highlight of being a basketball player. You know. So for me that was one of the big moments. Because it was such a underdog kind of thing. You know what I mean? It was really like we went against the music industry, we went against radio, you know, we went against all the things that are supposed to work. I used — all the music was live. Couldn’t get all the people together in one room. And so I actually cancelled — I stopped the record. I didn’t even, I was like I can’t get everybody together and I was like forget it, let’s just go on tour. So we went on tour. And in the middle of my tour my manager just called me and said, “I don’t know how it’s happened but all these people, all 20 people, their managers called me and they’re all available this one week.” So and that was the next week. So I canceled my tour from Europe. I canceled the week and I flew to L.A. and that’s why there’s so many cover songs on “Black Radio” — we did like half of the record is cover songs. Because I didn’t have anything written because it was so last minute. You know what I mean? So I did a bunch of covers because I didn’t have any songs. And a lot of the songs we did were on the spot. The song we did with Ledisi, we re-did one of my old joints, “F.T.B.” because she literally came to the studio at three in the morning and we sat around a table and she was like, “what do you want to play?” You know, and I was like, “I don’t know, what do you want to do?” And we threw out some songs na, um, na, not that. I said, “this song?” She said, “okay, cool.” We listened to it, wrote lyrics to it, [claps] went in the studio. With King, they were a new group. You know, and My Home-Grown was managing them. And I went to their creative and I had to do my laundry, because I just got back from tour. They had a laundry. So I literally walked into the studio in the living room and I came up with this little idea and I was like, “here’s the idea. I’m gonna do my laundry.” So I did laundry. And I came back, the song was done. I was like, “great.” No this is literally how the album got done. So I always tell people the universe co-produces your album. You know what I mean? I mean I’ve learned that for a long time. The universe will co-produce your album and when things are not going right it may be for the better, but it’s hard to realize that in the moment. But it may take a left turn for something you didn’t know. Like the “Ah Yeah” song. “Ah Yeah” is probably the one song I would say catapulted my career from one to another. © Fillius Jazz Archive -14-

Because the radio grabbed that song really quick and started playing it on the radio stations. So I started getting all these offers to do things. D’Angelo and Erykah Badu, but with people like Flying Lotus and Kendrick Lamar obviously and Chance the Rapper who are doing that a lot. And it’s becoming really big. What do you think is the cause of that at this time now in history, being such a big movement that’s happening right now?

Well I think there was two waves of it. I think there was one wave in the early or late 90s, the neo-soul movement. I was in New York when that happened. I didn’t realize it at the time but it was happening. I got to New York in ’97. I met Bilal in ’97. We started working with his album. I wasn’t into hard core hip-hop. I came from Texas. I knew Scarface. You know? I knew Ghetto Boys. So I was teaching Common piano lessons. I used to go to his house and give him piano lessons. He lived around the corner. Me, Bilal, Erykah and Common live within four blocks of each other in Brooklyn. So Erykah used to come over my crib and play me stuff, ideas, and, “what do you think about this song, ‘Orange Moon.’” I’m trying to think. Because I was the jazz guy. I was Bilal’s friend who played jazz. And they all was like, “what do you think about this jazz.” And Common was like, “I want to learn jazz.” You know. So I’d give him piano lessons. So that was all a regular thing for me. And I think it was just like a movement. The neo-soul movement happened and live musicians came back and poetry started popping then in ’97.
Spoken word.
